message.content: {"summary":"You achieved the top mark in every criterion. Your report names several ethical issues, ties them to engineering design and organisational context, and maps stakeholders in Table 1. Arguments for and against shipping are balanced and evidenced with quantitative external cases, and Figure 1's decision rule leads logically to options B and C and stakeholder-specific recommendations. Keep the explicit acknowledgement of the WannaCry analogue's limits — that candour strengthens the analysis.","next_steps":["Sustain the Excellent standard by keeping every conclusion sentence traceable to a named argument, as you do when you say Options B and C 'respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme'.","In RECOMMENDATIONS, add one line per stakeholder linking the recommendation back to the specific argument it answers, so the management, health department, chip supplier and product engineer actions read as a matched set.","Keep using Table 1, Table 2 and Figure 1 to carry argumentative weight rather than decorate; when you next revise, check each visual is referenced in the text at the point it advances the case."],"criteria":{"C1":"You open by framing design trade-offs as ethical ('Engineering design always trades quality against cost and time'), name test coverage being set by the release calendar, and Table 1 maps each stakeholder's interest and decision authority. Excellent requires both organisational context and stakeholder interest, and you show both. To hold this level, keep each stakeholder row explicitly tied to one of the three issues you list.","C2":"You balance the commercial case ('Shipping on time protects a real competitive advantage') against harm ('The strongest objection is harm to people who have no say'), then weigh Options B and C and give recommendations for Rachel, management, the health department, the chip supplier and product engineers. Excellent requires depth plus multi-stakeholder recommendations, which you meet. Next time, state in one sentence why B and C beat A and D.","C3":"Your structure builds cleanly from issues to arguments to the decision rule in Figure 1 to options and conclusion, and 'Three ethical issues follow' signposts the path. The conclusion is well supported and stakeholder consequences are mapped systematically, meeting Excellent. To keep this, ensure each recommendation in RECOMMENDATIONS names the argument it resolves.","C4":"You substantiate claims with quantitative evidence — 81 of 236 trusts disrupted and 19,000 appointments cancelled, Intel's US$475 million charge, Volkswagen's US$4.3 billion — and you explicitly acknowledge the WannaCry analogue's limits. Excellent requires both qualitative and quantitative evidence plus balanced, in-depth research, which you demonstrate. Continue flagging where an analogue only partly fits.","C5":"Your report is fluent and concise, uses abstract, introduction, body and conclusion, deploys Table 1, Table 2 and the Figure 1 flowchart competently, and follows IEEE-style referencing with relevant sources. That meets Excellent. To sustain it, keep each visual referenced in the text exactly where it advances the argument, and keep reference entries matched to the claims they support."}}
message.reasoning:
We need to produce JSON with summary (<=80 words), next_steps (3 strings), criteria object with each criterion id mapped to feedback <=70 words each. Address student as "you". Be specific, cite sections/figures, name what they did well, state what next rubric level requires. All criteria are Excellent at 10/10 — so next level is... there's no higher level. So for next steps, we should frame as "to consolidate/extend" — but rubric says don't change marks. We can say at Excellent, the next level would be sustaining this standard; but we should state what the next rubric level requires — since they're at the top, we can note that they're at the highest level and describe what maintaining it requires, or point to transferable improvements. Better: acknowledge top level achieved and describe what would keep it there / what distinguishes excellent from very good (i.e., what they must not lose). That's honest.

Let me write per-criterion feedback citing evidence.

C1: You open by framing design trade-offs as ethical ("Engineering design always trades quality against cost and time"), name test coverage driven by release calendar, and Table 1 maps stakeholders to interests and decision authority. Excellent requires both organisational context and stakeholder interest — you demonstrate both. To hold this, keep the stakeholder table tied explicitly to each issue.

C2: You balance commercial ("Shipping on time protects a real competitive advantage") against harm ("The strongest objection is harm to people who have no say"), then give options B and C and stakeholder-specific recommendations. Excellent requires depth plus recommendations for several stakeholders — met. Next: keep each recommendation explicitly linked to the argument it answers.

C3: Structure builds from issues → arguments → decision rule (Figure 1) → options → conclusion; "Three ethical issues follow" signposts. Systematic stakeholder mapping. To sustain Excellent, ensure every conclusion sentence traces to a named argument.

C4: Quantitative evidence (81 of 236 trusts, 19,000 appointments; Intel US$475m; VW US$4.3bn) plus acknowledged WannaCry analogue limitation. Excellent needs both qualitative and quantitative plus balanced in-depth research. Next: keep acknowledging limits of analogues explicitly, as you did.

C5: Abstract, intro, body, conclusion; Table 1, Table 2, Figure 1 flowchart; IEEE-style references. Fluent and concise. To hold Excellent, keep visuals doing argumentative work rather than decoration.

Summary <=80 words.

Next steps: 3 strings, actionable.

Let's write.
